subject: AI & Agents
title: Mixture of Experts: Smart Routing
description: A quick, practical guide to Mixture of Experts: Smart Routing.

hook.text: What if a massive model only used a fraction of itself for each question? That's mixture of experts.

buildup.text: Traditional models activate all parameters for every input, wasting compute on irrelevant neurons.

discovery.text: MoE models route each input to specialized sub-networks, using only relevant experts per query.

twist.text: GPT-4 is rumored to be a MoE model. Total parameters are huge, but active ones per query are modest.

climax.text: MoE lets models be both large and efficient — the best of both worlds for next-generation AI.

punchline.text: Don't wake every expert for every question. Ask the right one.

quiz.question: How do Mixture of Experts models improve efficiency?
options: They route each input to only the relevant specialist sub-networks
They use every parameter for every query
They reduce the total number of parameters

details.summary: Mixture of Experts models route each input to specialized sub-networks rather than processing everything through the entire model. This makes giant models faster and cheaper by only activating relevant experts.
details.whyItMatters: MoE enables building much larger models without proportionally increasing compute costs. It is a key architecture behind frontier models, making powerful AI more efficient and scalable.
takeaways: MoE routes inputs to specialized sub-networks called experts
Only a fraction of the model is active for each input
It enables scaling model size without scaling compute costs

faq.question: How does the routing in MoE models work?
faq.answer: A learned gating network examines each input and selects which experts should process it. Typically only 2-4 experts are activated out of dozens or hundreds, keeping compute costs low despite massive total model size.

faq.question: Which major AI models use Mixture of Experts?
faq.answer: GPT-4 and Mixtral are both rumored or confirmed to use MoE architectures. The approach is increasingly popular as a way to scale model capability while controlling inference costs.
